A rank-based comparison of more than two groups
Earlier, we used the Wilcoxon rank-sum test to compare two independent groups using the ranks of the observations rather than their numerical values.
The Kruskal–Wallis test extends this same rank-based idea to more than two independent groups.

The observations are pooled and ranked from smallest to largest, and we ask whether the groups tend to occupy different positions in the ranking.

The Kruskal–Wallis statistic does this by comparing the average ranks across groups.
This is done with the R function kruskal.test():

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

The small p-value suggests that the groups differ in where their observations tend to fall in the overall ranking.
As with the Wilcoxon rank-sum test, Kruskal–Wallis is not simply a test of population medians, nor should it be viewed simply as “ANOVA for non-normal data.”
If the group distributions have similar shapes, the test can be interpreted as a comparison of their locations.

title: Lecture 4: Designing and Analyzing Studies
text:
Power
Suppose we are comparing two populations and there really is a difference between their means:
\[\large
\mu_A = 10
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\mu_B = 12\]
so that the true population difference is
\[\large
\mu_B-\mu_A=2.\]
If we conduct a study comparing these two groups, will we necessarily detect the difference?
Let’s simulate a study with \(n\) observations in each group.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
We know that the population means differ by 2. But because of sampling variability, the estimated difference will vary from study to study.
If we repeated the study with new samples, sometimes the observed difference would be large enough to produce a small p-value, and sometimes it would not.

If a population difference really exists, how likely is our study to detect it?


Repeating the study
Instead of conducting the study once, let’s simulate it many times.
For each simulated study, we will:

sample \(n\) observations from each population;
estimate the difference between the group means;
conduct a two-sample t-test;
record whether \(p < 0.05\).


Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Let’s plot the observed \(t\)-values:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Each value in the histogram is the \(t\)-statistic from one simulated study. In every simulation, the population means differ by 2.
The blue region represents studies that reject \(H_0\); the gray region represents studies that fail to reject \(H_0\), even though the population means really are different.
The probability of rejecting the null hypothesis when a particular alternative is true is called power:
\[\large
\text{Power}
=
P(\text{reject } H_0 \mid \mu_B - \mu_A = 2)\]
The probability of failing to reject the null hypothesis when that alternative is true is the Type II error probability, denoted by \(\beta\):
\[\large
\beta
=
P(\text{fail to reject } H_0 \mid \mu_B - \mu_A = 2)\]
Therefore,
\[\large
\text{Power} = 1-\beta\]

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

A study does not have a single power independent of the effect. Power depends on the particular population difference we want the study to be able to detect.



What determines power?
Power increases when the population difference becomes large relative to the sampling variability of its estimate.
Let’s see how changes in the study affect power.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Increasing the sample size (\(n_A\) and \(n_B\)) reduces the sampling variability of the estimated difference:
\[
\large
SE(\bar Y_B-\bar Y_A)
=
\sqrt{\frac{\sigma_A^2}{n_A}+
\frac{\sigma_B^2}{n_B}}
\]

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Increasing the population standard deviations (\(\large \sigma_A\)and\(\large \sigma_B\)) increases the sampling variability of the estimated difference:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Increasing the population difference (\(\mu_B - \mu_A\)) increases power:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.


Power curves
We can put these relationships together in a set of power curves:

A power curve shows the probability of rejecting the null hypothesis across a range of possible population differences.
For any particular population difference, power depends on the sample size and the variability of the outcome.

Power also depends on the threshold we use for rejecting the null hypothesis. Increasing \(\alpha\) makes it easier to reject \(H_0\) and therefore increases power—but at the cost of increasing the probability of a Type I error. We generally specify \(\alpha\) in advance rather than choosing it as a way to increase power.



Standardized effect size
The simulations show that power depends both on the size of the population difference and on the variability of the outcome.
A difference of 2 units is relatively large when the population standard deviation is 3, but relatively small when the standard deviation is 10.
One way to express the size of a difference relative to the variability is the standardized mean difference:
\[\large d = \frac{\mu_B-\mu_A}{\sigma}\]
For our example,
\[\large d = \frac{12-10}{3} = 0.67.\]
This standardized effect size is often called Cohen’s \(d\).
Standardized effect sizes express the population difference relative to the variability of the outcome and are particularly useful in power and sample-size calculations.
However, when the original units are scientifically meaningful, a difference expressed in those units is often easier to interpret.


From power to sample size
Before conducting a study, we usually face the problem in the opposite direction.
We specify a population difference that would be important to detect and ask:

How large a sample do we need to have a reasonable chance of detecting that difference?

We can calculate the required sample size using power.t.test() in R.
Suppose a difference of 2 units is scientifically meaningful, we expect the population SD to be approximately 3, and we want an 80% probability of rejecting \(H_0\) if the true population difference is 2, using \(\alpha = 0.05\). What is the target sample size for each group?

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
power.t.test() calculates analytically the same quantity that we estimated through simulation.
Alternatively, the pwr.t.test() function in the pwr package specifies the population difference using Cohen’s \(d\). In this case,
\[\large
d = \frac{\Delta}{\sigma} = \frac{2}{3}.\]

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
The two approaches give essentially the same result; Cohen’s \(d\) simply combines the population difference and SD into a single standardized quantity.

Sample size calculations require us to specify what population difference matters scientifically and how likely we want the study to be to detect that difference.

section: What are we trying to learn?
text:
What are we trying to learn?
Hypothesis testing is often used to make a binary decision:

Do we reject \(H_0\) or fail to reject \(H_0\)?

But often we care more about:

How large is the estimated difference or association?
How uncertain are we about that estimate?

Reducing the scientific finding to p<0.05 can obscure both.

Shift the focus from testing to estimation.

Revisiting our birth weight analysis with a focus on estimation of mean

A sample mean \(\bar{x}\) is our point estimate of the population mean \(\mu\).
But another random sample would give us a different estimate.
The standard error tells us how much \(\bar{x}\) varies from sample to sample.
A confidence interval uses this sampling variability to quantify the uncertainty in our estimate of \(\mu\).


Constructing a 95% confidence interval
From Lecture 2, we know that when \(\sigma\) is unknown, the standardized sample mean follows a t-distribution.

What does 95% confidence mean?
The general formulation of the 95% confidence interval is
\[
\large

\times
\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}
\]

The population mean \(\mu\) is fixed.
The interval changes from sample to sample.
About 95% of intervals constructed this way contain \(\mu\).
A particular interval either contains \(\mu\) or it does not.


95% confidence describes the long-run performance of the procedure, not a 95% probability that \(\mu\) lies in this particular interval.

The confidence interval quantifies the uncertainty around our estimate and gives a range of parameter values that are reasonably consistent with the observed data.

text:
Relaxing the assumption of normality
The usual small-sample t-test results are exact when the populations are normally distributed.
But how well does the t-test perform when the populations are not normal?
We can use simulation to examine how the t-test behaves when the populations are not normally distributed.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

How robust is the two-sample t-test?
We can use simulation to examine how the t-test behaves when its normality assumption is violated.
For each simulation:

Generate two independent samples from the same population.
Conduct a two-sample Welch t-test at \(\alpha = 0.05\).
Record whether the null hypothesis is rejected.
Repeat the process many times.

Because the two samples come from the same population, the null hypothesis is true.

If the test is performing as expected, it should incorrectly reject the null hypothesis about 5% of the time

title: Lecture 3: Estimation and Uncertainty
text:
Rank-based methods
An alternative way to compare two populations
The t-test compares population means using the actual outcome values.
An alternative is to compare the relative ordering of observations between groups without allowing a few extreme values to dominate the comparison.
The Wilcoxon rank-sum test compares the relative ordering of observations:

Combine the observations from the two groups.
Rank them from smallest to largest.
Keep track of which group each observation came from.
Compare the ranks between the two groups.

If observations from one population tend to be larger, they will tend to have higher ranks.

The Wilcoxon rank-sum test is not simply a t-test for non-normal data—it provides a different way of comparing two populations.

The test uses ranks to assess whether observations from one population tend to be larger or smaller than observations from the other.
When the distributions have the same shape, the comparison can be interpreted as a test of a location shift.

In many settings, the t-test and Wilcoxon rank-sum test …
will lead to the same practical conclusion. For example, if a treatment generally shifts outcomes upward, it will usually increase both the population mean and the tendency for treated observations to be higher than control observations.
But the two comparisons can diverge when treatment changes the distribution in more complicated ways:

A treatment might produce very large improvements in a small number of patients, substantially increasing the mean without making outcomes better for most patients.
A treatment might primarily change the variability of the outcome, without substantially changing either the mean or the tendency for observations in one group to be higher.


The scientific question should determine what kind of difference between the populations we care about; the observed shape of the data should not simply determine which test we use.

title: Lecture 3: Estimation and Uncertainty
section: Binary outcomes - estimating a population proportion
text:
Binary outcomes - estimating a population proportion
For a binary outcome, each observation can take one of two values, such as:

Yes / No
Success / Failure
Event / No event

For a binary outcome \(X\),
\[\large
E(X) = p
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(X) = p(1-p).
\]
Since the sample proportion \(\hat{p}\) is simply the mean of \(n\) binary observations,
\[\large
\hat{p} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i,\]
its variance is
\[\large
\operatorname{Var}(\hat{p})
=
\frac{p(1-p)}{n}.\]

A sample proportion is simply a sample mean when the outcome is coded 0/1.

Since \(\hat{p}\) is a sample mean, the Central Limit Theorem applies.
For sufficiently large samples, the sampling distribution of \(\hat{p}\) is approximately normal, with estimated standard error
\[\large
\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}(\hat{p})
=
\sqrt{
\frac{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})}{n}
}.\]
This gives us the familiar form for a 95% confidence interval:
\[\large
\text{estimate}
\ \pm\
\text{critical value}
\times
\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}\]
or, using the normal approximation,
\[\large
\hat{p}
\ \pm\
1.96
\sqrt{
\frac{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})}{n}
}\]

The confidence interval quantifies the uncertainty around our estimate of the population proportion.


When is the normal approximation reasonable?
The normal approximation works best when there are sufficient numbers of both possible outcomes.
A common rule of thumb is to have at least 10 observed events and 10 observed non-events:
\[\large
n\hat{p} \geq 10
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
n(1-\hat{p}) \geq 10.\]

This is a guideline, not a threshold. The quality of the approximation changes gradually and depends on both the sample size and the population proportion.

When one of the outcomes is rare, a much larger sample may therefore be needed for the normal approximation to work well.

Suppose 40 of 100 patients experience an outcome.

Based on this sample, we estimate that 40% of the population experiences the outcome, with a 95% confidence interval of approximately 30% to 50%.

title: Lecture 3: Estimation and Uncertainty
text:
Comparing two population proportions
We are conducting a behavioral experiment on rats and want to compare trial success rates across two groups.

In Group 1, 35 of 48 rats complete the test successfully.
In Group 2, 27 of 52 rats complete the test successfully.

How much does the probability of success differ between the two populations?
The estimated success proportions are
\[\large \hat{p}_1 = \frac{35}{48} = 0.729\] and
\[\large \hat{p}_2 = \frac{27}{52} = 0.519.\]
The estimated difference in proportions is
\[\large
\hat{p}_1-\hat{p}_2
=
0.729-0.519
=
0.210.
\]
So the observed success rate is about 21 percentage points higher in Group 1.

Confidence interval for the difference
The estimated standard error is
\[
\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}(\hat{p}_1-\hat{p}_2)
=
\sqrt{
\frac{\hat{p}_1(1-\hat{p}_1)}{n_1}
+
\frac{\hat{p}_2(1-\hat{p}_2)}{n_2}
}.
\]

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

We estimate that the success probability is about 21 percentage points higher in Group 1, with a 95% confidence interval ranging from 2.5 to 39.5 percentage points higher.



Testing equality of two population proportions
We can also test \[
\large
H_0:p_1=p_2
\]
against
\[\large
H_A:p_1\neq p_2.
\]
Under the null hypothesis, the two populations have a common proportion \(p\).
We estimate this common proportion by pooling the observations from the two groups:
\[
\large
\hat{p}
=
\frac{x_1+x_2}{n_1+n_2}.
\]
The standard error under the null hypothesis is
\[
\large
\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}_0
=
\sqrt{
\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})
\left(
\frac{1}{n_1}
+
\frac{1}{n_2}
\right)
}.
\]
The test statistic is therefore
\[
\large
z
=
\frac{
(\hat{p}_1-\hat{p}_2)-0
}{
\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}_0
}.\]> For the confidence interval, we estimate variability using the observed proportion in each group. For the hypothesis test, we estimate variability assuming the null hypothesis is true:\(\large p_1=p_2\).

Comparing observed and expected counts
We now compare what we observed with what we would expect if group and outcome were not associated.
For each cell, its contribution to the chi-square statistic is
\[

\] where \(O_{ij}\)is the observed count and \(E_{ij}\) is the expected count.

Squaring ensures that deviations in either direction contribute positively.

From the chi-square statistic to a p-value
If group and outcome are not associated, the chi-square statistic has approximately a chi-square distribution.
The degrees of freedom for an \(r\times c\) contingency table are

title: Lecture 5: Modeling Continuous Outcomes
section: From comparing groups to modeling a relationship
text:
From comparing groups to modeling a relationship
Can we describe how mean blood pressure changes continuously with age?
We already know how to compare mean outcomes across groups. For example, we could divide people into age groups and compare mean blood pressure across those groups.
But age is not naturally a group variable. It is quantitative.

Can we describe how mean blood pressure changes continuously with age?

We will start with simulated data so that we know exactly how the population was generated.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
What does the plot suggest?

Older people tend to have higher systolic blood pressure.
But there is substantial variation among people of the same or similar age.


We could create groups…
One approach would be to divide age into categories.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
We could then compare mean systolic blood pressure across the three groups, perhaps using ANOVA.
But this throws away information.
Someone who is 40 and someone who is 59 are treated as belonging to the same age group, while someone who is 39 and someone who is 40 are treated as belonging to different groups.
The grouping is arbitrary: different cut points would give us different groups and different summaries.

Rather than asking how mean blood pressure differs across age groups, we would like to describe how mean blood pressure changes with age.

title: Lecture 5: Modeling Continuous Outcomes
text:
Modeling the mean outcome
Because we generated these data ourselves, we know the population relationship:
\[\large
E(\text{SBP}\mid\text{age}) =
100 + 0.5(\text{age})\]
The left-hand side refers to the mean systolic blood pressure among people of a particular age.
For example, at age 40:
\[\large
E(\text{SBP}\mid\text{age}=40)
=
100 + 0.5(40)
=
120\]
At age 60:
\[\large
E(\text{SBP}\mid\text{age}=60)
=
100 + 0.5(60)
=
130\]
So the slope tells us that:

For each additional year of age, mean systolic blood pressure increases by 0.5 mm Hg.

More generally, a simple linear regression model describes the population mean of an outcome as
\[\large
E(Y\mid X=x)
=
\beta_0+\beta_1x\]
where

\(\beta_0\) is the intercept
\(\beta_1\) is the slope

The slope \(\beta_1\) describes the change in mean \(Y\) associated with a one-unit increase in \(X\).

\(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\) are population parameters that we will estimate using a sample.


The mean is not an individual outcome
Let’s add the population mean relationship to the data.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
The line does not tell us the blood pressure of any particular person.
It describes the mean blood pressure at each age.
Individual observations vary around that mean.
We can write this as
\[\large
Y_i
=
\beta_0+\beta_1X_i+\epsilon_i\]
For our simulated data,
\[\large
\text{SBP}_i
=
100 + 0.5(\text{age}_i) + \epsilon_i\]
where
\[\large
\epsilon_i \sim N(0,12^2)\]

The model separates the mean relationship between X and Y from the individual variation around that mean.



Changing the population relationship
Because this is simulated data, we can change the population and see what happens.
For example, what would happen if there were no relationship between age and mean blood pressure?
We can use the function to visualize different scenarios:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
These parameters describe different features of the population:
\[\large
\beta_1
\quad\longrightarrow\quad
\text{how the mean changes with }X\]
\[\large
\sigma
\quad\longrightarrow\quad
\text{how much individuals vary around that mean}\]

title: Lecture 5: Modeling Continuous Outcomes
text:
Estimating the regression line

In a real study, we do not know the population line
In the simulation we knew that
\[\large
\beta_0=100,\qquad
\beta_1=0.5,\qquad
\sigma=12\]
because we generated the data.
In a real study, these population quantities are unknown.
We only observe a sample:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
So our next statistical question is:

How can we use the observed data to estimate the unknown population regression line?



How well does a line fit the data?
Suppose we propose the following line:
\[\large
\widehat{\text{SBP}}
=
95 + 0.6(\text{age})\]
For each person, the line gives us a fitted value. The difference between the observed and fitted value is called the residual.
\[\large
e_i
=
Y_i-\hat{Y}_i\]
We can visualize these residuals as the vertical distances between the observed values and the proposed line.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Some residuals are positive and some are negative.
A line that fits the data well should generally have small residuals.


What criterion should we use to choose a line?
There are infinitely many lines we could draw through the data.
How should we evaluate each line? Simply adding the residuals will not work because positive and negative residuals can cancel each other out.

Proposal: try to minimize the sum of squared residuals:

\[\large
SSE = \sum_{i=1}^{n} e_i^2
=
\sum_{i=1}^{n}
(Y_i-\hat{Y}_i)^2\]
Let’s start with some possible lines and take a look at the SSE for each:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Can we do better?


Finding the minimum
Least squares finds the line that minimizes the sum of squared residuals (SSE).
We do not need to calculate this solution ourselves. R can find the values of the intercept and slope for us.

The least-squares regression line is the line that makes the sum of squared residuals as small as possible.


Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
The fitted line has a lower SSE than all of our guesses—and, in fact, the lowest SSE of any possible line!
The fitted regression equation is
\[\large
\widehat{\text{SBP}}
=
\hat{\beta}_0+
\hat{\beta}_1(\text{age})\]
where \(\hat{\beta}_0\) and \(\hat{\beta}_1\) are estimates of the unknown population parameters \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\).


Estimated versus population relationship
Because these data were simulated, we have an advantage that we would not have with real data: we know the true population relationship.
Let’s compare it with the relationship estimated from our sample.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
The two lines are not exactly the same.
The population parameters are
\[\large
\beta_0=100,
\qquad
\beta_1=0.5\]
while our sample gives estimates
\[\large
\hat{\beta}_0
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\hat{\beta}_1.\]

The estimated regression line differs from the population regression line because of sampling variability.

If we collected another random sample from the same population, we would get a somewhat different regression line.
So what would happen if we repeated this study many times?

title: Lecture 5: Modeling Continuous Outcomes
section: Sampling variability of the estimated slope
text:
Sampling variability of the estimated slope
From our sample, we estimated a slope \(\hat{\beta}_1\).
But this was only one random sample from the population.
When we collect another sample from exactly the same population, we should get different observations and a somewhat different estimate of the slope.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
The estimated slope is not exactly the same as the one from our first sample.
That’s sampling variability — the same phenomenon we have seen throughout the course.

What happens across many samples?
Now let’s repeat the study many times.
Each time we will:

draw a new sample of 200 people from the same population
fit the same linear regression model
save the estimated regression line


Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Each repeated study produces a somewhat different estimated regression line.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
All of these samples came from the same population, but sampling variability produces somewhat different estimated regression lines.


The sampling distribution of the slope
Each estimated regression line has its own estimated slope \(\hat{\beta}_1\).
Remember, the true population slope is
\[\large
\beta_1 = 0.5\]
Let’s look at the distribution of the estimated slopes.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
The estimates vary from sample to sample, but they are centered around the true population slope.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
The standard deviation of this sampling distribution tells us how much the estimated slope typically varies from sample to sample.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
This is the standard error of the estimated slope.
\[\large
SE(\hat{\beta}_1)
=
SD\left(\text{sampling distribution of }\hat{\beta}_1\right)\]


Inference for the slope
In a real study, we have only one sample, so we cannot observe the sampling distribution directly.
Instead, we use our sample to estimate the standard error of \(\hat{\beta}_1\).

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
The standard error reported by the regression model estimates the sampling variability that we observed directly through simulation.
Once we have an estimate and its standard error, the rest should look familiar.
To test
\[\large
H_0:\beta_1=0,\]
we calculate
\[\large
t\text{-statistic}
=
\frac{\hat{\beta}_1-0}
{SE(\hat{\beta}_1)}\]
This has exactly the same structure we have seen before:
\[\large
\frac{\text{estimate}-\text{null value}}
{\text{standard error}}\]
And we can construct a confidence interval for the population slope:
\[\large
\hat{\beta}_1
\ \pm\
t_{\text{critical}}SE(\hat{\beta}_1)\]
R provides these quantities directly.

title: Lecture 5: Modeling Continuous Outcomes
text:
Regression with a categorical predictor
So far, our predictor has been quantitative. But predictors can also be categorical.
Suppose we want to compare mean outcomes between two groups.

We already know how to compare these groups using a two-sample t-test:

section: Multiple regression: accounting for another variable
text:
Multiple regression: accounting for another variable
Up until this point, our regression models have contained one predictor at a time.
But outcomes are often associated with several characteristics simultaneously.
Suppose we are primarily interested in the relationship between physical activity and systolic blood pressure.
But age may also matter:

older people tend to have higher systolic blood pressure
physical activity may differ with age

So if age and physical activity are related, a simple comparison of blood pressure across activity levels may partly reflect differences in age.
We will again use simulation so that we know exactly how the population was generated.
Suppose the population is generated according to:
\[\large
\begin{aligned}
\text{activity}_i
&= 8 - 0.06\,\text{age}_i + \epsilon_{Ai}, \quad \epsilon_{Ai} \sim N(0, 1.5^2) \\[6pt]
\text{SBP}_i
&= 105 + 0.55\,\text{age}_i - 2\,\text{activity}_i + \epsilon_{Yi}, \quad \epsilon_{Yi} \sim N(0, 10^2)
\end{aligned}\]
In this population:

mean SBP is higher with increasing age
mean SBP is lower with greater physical activity
older people tend to be less physically active


Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

Let’s first look at the relationship between activity and blood pressure
First the plot:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
We can fit the simple regression:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
This gives the unadjusted association between activity and mean systolic blood pressure.


Accounting for age
But we know how this population was generated: age is related to both activity and blood pressure.
So our simple regression compares people with different activity levels who may also differ systematically in age.

Can we estimate the association between activity and blood pressure while accounting for age?

For intuition, let’s temporarily compare the activity–SBP relationship among people of similar ages.
We are grouping age only for visualization; in the regression model, age will remain quantitative.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
The colored lines compare activity and SBP among people of roughly similar ages. The dashed line is the overall, unadjusted relationship.


What does that mean with quantitative age?
Multiple regression allows us to account for age without dividing it into groups.
Let’s break down the intuition. (This is not what you actually have to do in practice).
First, we model physical activity as a function of age, and gather the residuals:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Someone above the line is more active than expected for their age; someone below the line is less active than expected for their age.
The residual is the vertical difference between the observed activity and the activity expected for that person’s age:
\[\large
\text{activity residual}
=
\text{observed activity}
-
\text{activity expected for age}\]
Likewise, we can calculate an SBP residual that tells us how much higher or lower someone’s blood pressure is than expected for their age:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Now we compare:

activity relative to what we expect for age, with
SBP relative to what we expect for age.


Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
We can estimate the age-adjusted relationship between activity and SBP using these residuals:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Multiple regression estimates this relationship directly:
\[\large
E(SBP \mid \text{age, activity}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \times \text{age} + \beta_2 \times \text{activity}\]

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
The activity coefficient is exactly the slope we obtained using the residuals.
The activity coefficient \(\beta_2\) in the full model describes the association between activity and mean SBP after accounting for age, using the variation in activity that is not explained by its linear relationship with age.
Because we simulated the population, we know that the age-adjusted activity coefficient is −2. Our estimate is quite close to the true population value.

section: What if predictors are highly correlated?
text:
What if predictors are highly correlated?
We just saw that the adjusted activity coefficient uses the variation in activity that remains after accounting for age.
But what happens if age and activity are very strongly related?
Let’s create a new population where activity is much more closely related to age.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
We can quantify the strength of these relationships using the correlation:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
When age and activity are highly correlated, there is much less variation in activity among people of similar ages.
That means there is less independent information available to estimate the separate associations of age and activity with SBP.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
In both populations, the true activity coefficient is
\[\large
\beta_{\text{activity}}=-2.\]

High correlation between predictors . . .

does not by itself bias the regression coefficients
provides less information for estimating their separate associations with the outcome
results in standard errors and wider confidence intervals
at the extreme, if two predictors are perfectly correlated, their separate associations cannot be estimated

This loss of precision is sometimes summarized by the variance inflation factor (VIF), which describes how much the variance of a coefficient is increased because a predictor is related to the other predictors in the model.
So, high correlation is primarily a precision problem.
But removing a highly correlated predictor is not necessarily the solution:

precision may improve
important differences that predictor accounts for may no longer be accounted for


Variables should not be removed simply because they are highly correlated. Which variables belong in the model depends on the scientific question and what the coefficient is intended to estimate.

section: Does the model adequately describe the data?
text:
Does the model adequately describe the data?
We can always fit a linear regression model. But fitting a model does not mean that the model provides a good description of the data.
How can we tell?
Let’s return to simulation, where we know exactly how the population was generated.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Here the population mean really is linear:
\[\large
E(Y\mid X)=20+3X\]
and the variability around that mean is the same throughout the range of \(X\).
Let’s fit a linear regression model.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
The fitted line appears to provide a reasonable description of how the mean outcome changes with \(X\).
But we can learn more by looking at what the model did not explain.

Looking at the residuals
Recall that a residual is the difference between an observed and fitted value:
\[\large
e_i=Y_i-\hat{Y}_i\]
If the model adequately describes the systematic relationship in the data, there should not be much systematic structure left in the residuals.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
What are we looking for?

Ideally, the residual plot should be fairly boring.

The residuals should be scattered around zero without an obvious systematic pattern.
A pattern in the residuals suggests that there is structure in the data that our model has not adequately captured.
So model checking is not simply a matter of passing a set of formal tests. We want to ask:

Does the fitted model provide a reasonable description of the data, and is there systematic information left in the residuals?



What if the mean relationship is not linear?
Now suppose the true population relationship is curved rather than linear.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Let’s fit a linear regression anyway.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
The linear model can still be fit, but the straight line does not adequately describe how the mean of \(Y\) changes with \(X\).
What do the residuals look like?

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Now the residual plot is not boring.
There is a systematic pattern: the model tends to overestimate the mean outcome in some parts of the range and underestimate it in others.

A pattern in the residuals can reveal structure in the mean relationship that the fitted model has failed to capture.



What if the variability changes?
A linear model describes both the mean relationship and the variability of observations around that mean.
So far, we have assumed that this variability is approximately constant across values of \(X\).
But suppose the mean relationship is still linear while the variability increases with \(X\).

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Here the linear model correctly describes the population mean:
\[\large
E(Y\mid X)=20+3X.\]
But the variability around that mean increases as \(X\) increases.
What does this look like in the residuals?

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Unlike the curved example, there is no systematic pattern in the mean of the residuals.
Instead, their spread increases as the fitted values increase.

The mean model may be appropriate even when the variability around that mean is not constant.

Why does this matter?
The least-squares estimates of the regression coefficients can still be appropriate, but the usual standard errors, confidence intervals, and p-values rely on assumptions about the variability of the errors.
So nonconstant variance is primarily a problem for inference, rather than evidence that the estimated mean relationship itself is wrong.


What about normality?
Linear regression is often described as requiring “normally distributed data.”
That is not quite right:

the predictor \(X\) does not need to be normally distributed
the outcome \(Y\) does not need to be normally distributed
the normality assumption concerns the errors around the conditional mean

\[\large
\epsilon_i \mid X_i \sim N(0,\sigma^2)\]
At any particular value of \(X\), individual outcomes are assumed to be normally distributed around the regression line.
We cannot observe the population errors, but we can examine the residuals.
One common tool is a normal Q-Q plot:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
If the residuals are approximately normally distributed, the points should fall roughly along a straight line.


How much does normality matter?

small departures from normality are common
they do not automatically make linear regression inappropriate
normality matters primarily for the usual small-sample inference about regression coefficients
with reasonably samples, inference is generally fairly robust to moderate departures from normality


We will not use formal tests of residual normality as a rule for deciding whether a linear regression model can be used.



Can individual observations strongly affect the model?
Observations can be “unusual” for a number of different reasons:

Large residual: unusual outcome given the predictors
High leverage: unusual predictor values
High influence: observation substantially affects the fitted model

These ideas are related, but they are not the same.
Let’s add one observation to our earlier data.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
The added observation has high leverage because its value of \(X\) is far from the other observations.
It also does not follow the relationship seen in the rest of the data. Together, these features make the observation influential: including it substantially changes the fitted regression line.

An unusual observation is not automatically an observation that should be deleted.

It may represent a data error, an unusual but legitimate individual, or evidence that our model does not adequately describe part of the population. We should investigate unusual observations before deciding what to do.


Identifying leverage and influence
Leverage measures how unusual an observation’s predictor values are:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
High leverage does not necessarily mean high influence. An observation can have unusual predictor values but still follow the overall relationship closely.
Cook’s distance measures influence — how much an observation affects the fitted regression model:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

Leverage asks whether the predictors are unusual. Cook’s distance asks whether the observation substantially affects the fitted model.

Both are tools for identifying observations worth investigating — not automatic rules for removing observations.

title: Lecture 5: Modeling Continuous Outcomes
text:
What should we actually check?
When we fit a regression model, we want to ask whether the model provides a reasonable description of the data.
Some useful steps are:

Look at the data and the fitted model. Does the estimated relationship appear to describe the observed data reasonably well?
Look at residuals versus fitted values. Systematic patterns may indicate that the mean relationship has not been adequately modeled; changes in spread may indicate nonconstant variance.
Consider unusual observations. Large residuals, high leverage, or high Cook’s distance may identify observations worth investigating.
Consider the distribution of the residuals, particularly when the sample is small and inference depends more strongly on the normality assumption.

Small departures from an idealized model are common. The important question is whether they are enough to meaningfully affect our estimates, uncertainty, or conclusions.

What if we find a problem?
What we do depends on what the problem is.

A systematic pattern in the residuals may indicate that we need a different model for the mean.
Nonconstant variability may require a different approach to estimating uncertainty.
Moderate departures from normality often require no action, particularly in samples.
Unusual or influential observations should be investigated, not automatically removed.


Diagnostics help us identify ways in which a model may be inadequate. The appropriate response depends on the nature of the problem and the question we are asking.

title: Biostatistics Lectures
text:
Multiple testing
Suppose we conduct a randomized study comparing a treatment with a control group.
We have 20 different outcomes and a separate research question for each:

Does treatment affect this outcome?

For each outcome \(j\):
\[\large
H_{0j}: \mu_{j1} - \mu_{j0} = 0,
\qquad j=1,\ldots,20\]
where \(\mu_{j1}\) and \(\mu_{j0}\) are the population means for outcome \(j\) in the treatment and control groups.
Suppose all 20 null hypotheses are true — treatment has no effect on any of the outcomes.
For any one test with \(\alpha=0.05\), the probability of a Type I error is 5%.
But we are conducting 20 tests.

How likely are we to find at least one statistically significant effect and conclude that the treatment “works”?


Simulating the study
Let’s simulate this study under the assumption that all 20 null hypotheses are true.
For each outcome, we will generate data from the same population distribution for the treatment and control groups:
\[\large
Y_{j1},Y_{j0} \sim N(45,3)\]
We will then test for a treatment effect separately for each of the 20 outcomes.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

One simulated study doesn’t tell us how often this happens. What if we repeat the entire study many times?



Let’s repeat the study many times . . .
In every simulated study:

all 20 null hypotheses are true
we test each outcome using \(\alpha=0.05\)
we record how many null hypotheses are rejected


Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

In about 64% of studies, at least one of the 20 tests is statistically significant.
Each individual test still has a 5% Type I error rate.
But across the family of 20 tests, the probability of making at least one Type I error is much larger than 5%.
The probability of making at least one Type I error across the family is called the family-wise error rate (FWER):

\[\large
\text{FWER} = P(\text{at least one Type I error})\]
For 20 independent tests, the probability that we make no Type I errors is
\[\large
(1-0.05)^{20}=0.95^{20}\approx0.36\]
so
\[\large
P(\text{at least one Type I error})
=1-0.95^{20}
\approx0.64.\]


Visualizing the problem
It is easier to see what is happening if we consider a smaller family of 5 outcomes.
The figure shows 100 simulated studies. In each study:

all 5 null hypotheses are true
each vertical line is a 95% confidence interval
a red interval does not include 0 and represents a Type I error
shaded columns identify studies with at least one Type I error


The expected Type 1 error rate with 5 outcomes is:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.


Controlling the family-wise error rate
We would like the probability of making at least one Type I error across all 20 tests to be no more than 5%.

Can we change the significance level for each individual test so that the FWER is controlled at 5%?

One simple approach is the Bonferroni correction.
Instead of testing each hypothesis using \(\alpha=0.05\), divide \(\alpha\) by the number of tests:
\[\large
\alpha^*=\frac{\alpha}{m}\]
where \(m\) is the number of tests.
For our 20 outcomes:
\[\large
\alpha^*=\frac{0.05}{20}=0.0025\]
We now reject an individual null hypothesis only when \(p < 0.0025\):

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
The Bonferroni correction controls the FWER because each individual test now has a Type I error probability of only 0.0025:
\[\large
\text{FWER}
\leq
20(0.0025)
=
0.05\]
The \(\leq\) is important:

Bonferroni guarantees that the FWER is no greater than 5% — it does not have to be exactly 5%.
Unlike \(1-(0.95)^{20}\), Bonferroni does not require the tests to be independent.
This is useful because outcomes in the same study are often correlated.

But there is a tradeoff:

By making it harder to reject each null hypothesis, Bonferroni also makes it harder to detect real effects.



The Holm procedure
Suppose we conduct five tests and obtain these ordered p-values:
\[\large
0.003,\quad 0.009,\quad 0.015,\quad 0.031,\quad 0.20\]
With Bonferroni, every p-value is compared with
\[\large
\frac{0.05}{5}=0.01.\]
Only the first two null hypotheses would be rejected.
Holm starts with the same threshold, but becomes progressively less stringent:

compare the smallest p-value with \(0.05/5\)
if rejected, compare the next with \(0.05/4\)
continue until a p-value fails to meet its threshold

Once a p-value fails to meet its threshold, the procedure stops.
Here, Bonferroni rejects 2 hypotheses; Holm rejects 3.

Holm controls the FWER just as Bonferroni does, but can have greater power.


Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Once the p-values have been adjusted, we compare them with the original significance level. In this case:

Reject the null hypothesis if the adjusted p-value is less than 0.05.


When all of the null hypotheses are true, Holm and Bonferroni have the same probability of making at least one rejection. Holm gains power after the first rejection by using progressively less stringent thresholds.

For controlling the FWER, Holm is generally preferred to Bonferroni because it provides the same error control while being at least as powerful.


Connecting back to ANOVA
In ANOVA, we may want to compare all pairs of group means.
With four groups, there are six pairwise comparisons:
\[\large
\mu_1-\mu_2,\quad
\mu_1-\mu_3,\quad
\mu_1-\mu_4,\quad
\mu_2-\mu_3,\quad
\mu_2-\mu_4,\quad
\mu_3-\mu_4\]
These six comparisons form another family of hypothesis tests, so we again need to consider the FWER.

Bonferroni and Holm are general-purpose methods for controlling the FWER.
The Tukey method is designed specifically for the situation in which we want to make all pairwise comparisons among a set of group means.
Rather than treating the comparisons as unrelated tests, Tukey takes advantage of their common structure.
Without going into the details, Tukey uses the studentized range distribution, which essentially asks:


If all the population means were equal, how far apart might the most separated sample means be simply because of sampling variability?


Tukey uses this distribution to choose a critical value for the pairwise differences. This produces wider confidence intervals — and larger adjusted p-values — than we would get by treating each comparison separately, while controlling the FWER.

title: Biostatistics Lectures
text:
False discovery rate
So far, we have focused on the family-wise error rate:

FWER: How likely are we to make any false discoveries?

But there is another way to think about errors when we conduct many tests:

FDR: What is the expected proportion of our discoveries that will be false?

Suppose we are testing 10,000 genes to identify genes that may be associated with a disease.
Controlling the FWER means trying to keep the probability of making even one false discovery among the 10,000 tests below 5%.
Using Bonferroni, we would require
\[\large
p < \frac{0.05}{10{,}000}=0.000005.\]
That is an extremely stringent threshold — and may be more stringent than we need.
Instead, we might be willing to tolerate some false discoveries, as long as they represent only a small proportion of all the discoveries we make.

False discovery proportion
Among the results we call statistically significant — our discoveries — some may be:

true discoveries — there really is an effect
false discoveries — Type I errors

For a particular study, the false discovery proportion (FDP) is
\[\large
\text{FDP}
=
\frac{\text{number of false discoveries}}
{\text{total number of discoveries}}.\]
For example, if 8 of 100 discoveries are false:
\[\large
\text{FDP}=\frac{8}{100}=0.08.\]
But FDP describes what happened in one particular study.
The false discovery rate (FDR) is the expected FDP across repeated studies:
\[\large
\text{FDR}=E(\text{FDP}).\]
This gives us two different ways of controlling errors across repeated studies:

FWER: How likely are we to make any false discoveries?
FDR: What is the expected proportion of our discoveries that will be false?

Controlling the FDR at 5% does not mean that exactly 5% of the discoveries in every study will be false.

For each simulated study, we calculate the false discovery proportion.

The false discovery rate is the expected FDP across repeated studies:
\[\large
\text{FDR}=E(\text{FDP})\]

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.


Controlling the false discovery rate

Can we control the proportion of our discoveries that are false without being as stringent as controlling the probability of even one false discovery?

The Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure is designed to do just that.
Let’s first see what it does before looking at how it works.

Across repeated studies, the average FDP — the false discovery rate — is approximately 5%.


The Benjamini-Hochberg procedure
The Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure controls the false discovery rate.
Like Holm, BH begins by ordering the p-values from smallest to largest:
\[\large
p_{(1)} \leq p_{(2)} \leq \cdots \leq p_{(m)}.\]
Suppose we have five tests and want to control the FDR at 5%.
BH compares each ordered p-value with
\[\large
\frac{i}{m}(0.05),\]
where \(i\) is the position of the p-value in the ordered list.
For five tests, the thresholds are:

Unlike Holm, BH does not stop when an individual p-value fails its threshold.

The idea behind the increasing thresholds is that BH permits a larger p-value cutoff because FDR allows some false discoveries when there are more discoveries overall.
Here, BH supports three discoveries, so the cutoff is
\[\large

All three smallest p-values are below 0.03, so all three null hypotheses are rejected.
More generally, BH searches for the largest set of discoveries that satisfies the FDR criterion.

Unlike FWER control, the goal is not to avoid every false discovery — it is to control the expected proportion of discoveries that are false.

text:
Missing data
Suppose we want to estimate the average outcome in a population.
Our research question is:

What is the population mean outcome?

Ideally, we would observe all of the variables we planned to collect for every participant.
But in real studies, some data are often missing:

some participants may be missing the outcome
others may be missing baseline characteristics or other covariates


When does missing data create a problem for our analysis?


Starting with missing outcomes
Let’s start with a simple sampling process in which the outcome is missing for some participants.
We will simulate 1,000 participants:

a baseline health score \(X\), observed for everyone
mean outcome of 50 for a participant with \(X=0\)
outcome standard deviation of 10

The baseline health score is related to the outcome:
\[\large
X_i \sim N(0,1)\]
\[\large
Y_i = 50 + 5X_i + \epsilon_i,
\qquad
\epsilon_i \sim N(0,10)\]
Because we are simulating the data, we know the true population mean is 50.

What if outcomes disappear randomly?
Suppose each participant has a 30% chance of having a missing outcome.
The probability of missingness is unrelated to:

baseline health
the value of the outcome

Repeating the study
Now let’s repeat the sampling many times.
In each simulated study, we estimate the population mean using:

the complete data
the observed data after 30% of outcomes are missing


Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
On average, both analyses recover the true population mean of 50.
But the estimates based on the incomplete data vary more from study to study:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

Randomly losing outcomes costs us information and precision, but does not systematically shift the estimate of the population mean.

This type of missingness is called Missing Completely at Random (MCAR):

The probability that a value is missing does not depend on any observed or unobserved data.




What if missingness depends on something we observed?
Now suppose the probability that the outcome is missing depends on the participant’s baseline health score.
Participants with lower baseline health scores are more likely to have a missing outcome.
Because baseline health is observed for everyone, we know something about why the outcome is missing.

When missingness depends on an observed variable that is related to the outcome, simply analyzing the observed outcomes can produce a biased estimate of the population mean.

This type of missingness is called Missing at Random (MAR):

The probability that a value is missing may depend on observed data, but — after accounting for those observed data — does not depend on the missing value itself.




Using the information we observed
Under MAR, we have information that helps explain why some outcomes are missing.
In our example:

baseline health is observed for everyone
baseline health predicts the outcome
baseline health also predicts whether the outcome is missing


Can we use baseline health to recover the population mean?

First, we estimate the relationship between baseline health and the outcome using participants whose outcomes were observed:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
We can then use this model to predict the outcome for everyone in our sample based on their observed baseline health:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

Instead of averaging only over the selected group with observed outcomes, we used information from the full sample to estimate the population mean.

This is one example of a model-based approach to handling missing data under MAR.


Multiple imputation
Another common approach for handling missing data under MAR is multiple imputation.
Multiple imputation uses the observed data to create several plausible completed datasets, rather than treating any single prediction for a missing value as if it were known.
Each completed dataset is analyzed separately, and the results are then combined.
Because the missing values differ across the completed datasets, the final analysis reflects uncertainty about the data we did not observe.

Multiple imputation does not recover the missing values — it represents plausible values and our uncertainty about them using the information we did observe.



What if missingness depends on what we did not observe?
Now suppose the probability that an outcome is missing depends on the value of the outcome itself.
Participants with lower outcome values are more likely to have a missing outcome.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Here, participants with lower outcomes are systematically more likely to be missing, inflating our estimate of the population mean.
But there is an important difference from our previous example:

For participants whose outcomes are missing, we do not observe the information that explains why they are missing.


Repeating the study
Let’s again repeat the sampling process many times.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

When the probability of missingness depends on the missing outcome itself, the observed outcomes may systematically differ from the outcomes we did not observe.

This type of missingness is called Missing Not at Random (MNAR):

Even after accounting for the observed data, the probability that a value is missing depends on the value that is missing.




Can we tell whether data are MNAR?
Usually, we cannot determine from the observed data whether missingness is MAR or MNAR.
For participants with missing outcomes, we do not know what those outcomes would have been. Therefore, we cannot directly determine whether missingness depends on those unobserved values.
However, an MAR assumption may be more reasonable when we have good observed information about:

factors that predict whether data are missing
factors that predict the missing outcome

For example, if participants in poorer health are more likely to have missing outcomes, detailed measures of their health before the outcome is missing may help make an MAR assumption more plausible.

We cannot prove that data are MAR, but collecting and using variables that help explain both the outcome and missingness can make the assumption more reasonable.



Can observed information solve the problem?
We can try the same model-based approach we used under MAR:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

Under MNAR, observed variables may help, but they cannot fully account for missingness that still depends on the unobserved value itself.



What can we do about MNAR?
Because we cannot know the missing outcomes, there is no purely data-driven solution to MNAR.
Instead, we can conduct sensitivity analyses:

Make different assumptions about the missing outcomes and ask whether our conclusions change.

More formal statistical methods for MNAR follow the same basic principle: they require assumptions about the data we did not observe.


Missing data: putting it together

MCAR: Missingness does not depend on observed or unobserved data.

Analyzing the observed data may cost precision; in our example, it does not systematically shift the estimate.

MAR: Missingness can depend on information we observed.

We can use that observed information to help account for the missing data.

MNAR: Missingness still depends on information we did not observe.

Observed information may help, but additional assumptions are needed to account fully for the missing data.



The consequences of missing data depend on why the data are missing — not simply on how much data are missing.

title: Logistic regression
text:
From continuous to binary outcomes
In the last lecture, we used regression to describe how the mean of an outcome changes with a predictor.
For a continuous outcome \(Y\), we wrote:
\[\large
E(Y \mid X=x) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x\]
But many outcomes we care about are binary:

disease / no disease
hospitalized / not hospitalized
treatment success / treatment failure
alive / dead

Can we use the same regression framework when the outcome takes only two possible values?

title: Logistic regression
text:
A simulated population
Suppose we are interested in the relationship between age and hypertension.
For each person, define
\[\large
Y =
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{if the person has hypertension} \\
0 & \text{if the person does not have hypertension}
\end{cases}\]
Let’s simulate a population in which the probability of hypertension increases with age.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
We know the probability used to generate each person’s outcome because we created the population ourselves.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Each observed outcome is either 0 or 1. But our scientific question is not really whether a particular individual has hypertension.
We want to know:

How does the probability of hypertension change with age?

title: Logistic regression
section: The mean of a binary outcome is a probability
text:
The mean of a binary outcome is a probability
Recall that regression models the conditional mean:
\[\large
E(Y \mid X=x)\]
What does a mean represent when an outcome can only be 0 or 1?
Suppose that among 100 people of the same age, 30 have hypertension. If hypertension is coded 1 for yes and 0 for no, the mean is
\[\large
\bar{Y}
=
\frac{30(1)+70(0)}{100}
=
0.30\]
The mean is simply the proportion of people with hypertension.
In the population, that proportion is a probability. Therefore, for a binary outcome coded 0 and 1,
\[\large
E(Y \mid X=x)
=
P(Y=1 \mid X=x)\]
So for a binary outcome:

Modeling the conditional mean is the same thing as modeling the probability that \(Y=1\).

Because we simulated these data, we can see the true probability in the population.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

title: Logistic regression
text:
Can we use linear regression?
We want to model the probability of hypertension as a function of age.
We already know how to model a conditional mean. Why not just use linear regression?

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
The fitted model is
\[\large
E(Y \mid \text{age}) = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 \text{age}\]
Since \(E(Y \mid \text{age}) = P(Y=1 \mid \text{age})\), the fitted values from this model are estimates of the probability of hypertension.
Let’s compare the fitted linear model with the true probabilities we used to generate the data.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
The linear model captures the general idea that hypertension becomes more common with age, but it does not capture the shape of the relationship very well.

A straight line assumes that the probability changes by the same amount for every one-year increase in age.
But probabilities are constrained: \(0 \leq P(Y=1 \mid X) \leq 1\)
A linear model does not enforce this constraint. Depending on the predictor values, it can produce fitted probabilities below 0 or above 1.


What we need is a regression model that …

allows the probability to change with age
keeps predicted probabilities between 0 and 1
retains the basic structure of a linear regression model


How can we turn a probability, which is constrained between 0 and 1, into something we can model on an unrestricted linear scale?

title: Logistic regression
text:
From probabilities to odds
A probability is constrained to lie between 0 and 1.
One way to transform a probability is to express it as odds:
\[\large
\text{odds} = \frac{p}{1-p}\]
Odds compare the probability that an event occurs with the probability that it does not occur.
For example, if the probability of hypertension is 0.75,
\[\large
\text{odds} = \frac{0.75}{0.25} = 3\]
The odds of hypertension are 3 to 1: for every 3 people with hypertension, we would expect about 1 without hypertension.

From odds to log odds
Odds are no longer constrained to lie between 0 and 1:
\[\large
0 < \text{odds} < \infty\]
But they are still constrained — odds cannot be negative.
Taking the logarithm removes this constraint:
\[\large
\text{log odds} = \log\left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right)\]
The log odds can take any value:
\[\large
-\infty < \log\left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right) < \infty\]

title: Logistic regression
text:
Logistic regression
We now have a quantity that can range from \(-\infty\) to \(\infty\).
So instead of modeling the probability directly as a linear function of age, logistic regression models the log odds as a linear function of age:
\[\large
\log\left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right)
=
\beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{age}\]
where
\[\large
p = P(Y=1 \mid \text{age})\]

title: Logistic regression
section: From log odds back to probability
text:
From log odds back to probability
The logistic regression model is linear on the log-odds scale:
\[\large
\log\left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right)
=
\beta_0 + \beta_1 X\]

But we are usually more interested in the probability of the outcome than in its log odds.

We can transform the model back to the probability scale, first by exponentiating both sides: \[\large
\frac{p}{1-p}
=
\exp(\beta_0+\beta_1X)\]
Multiply both sides by \((1-p)\):
\[\large
p
=
(1-p)\exp(\beta_0+\beta_1X)\]
Collect the terms involving \(p\):
\[\large
p + p\exp(\beta_0+\beta_1X)
=
\exp(\beta_0+\beta_1X)\]
Factor out \(p\):
\[\large
p\left[1+\exp(\beta_0+\beta_1X)\right]
=
\exp(\beta_0+\beta_1X)\]
So
\[\large
p
=
\frac{\exp(\beta_0+\beta_1X)}
{1+\exp(\beta_0+\beta_1X)}\]
which is equivalent to
\[\large
p
=
\frac{1}
{1+\exp[-(\beta_0+\beta_1X)]}\]
This transformation guarantees that the predicted probability remains between 0 and 1, regardless of the values of \(X\), \(\beta_0\), or \(\beta_1\).

You do not need to reproduce this algebra. The important point is that the probability curve follows directly from the linear model for the log odds.

This is where the probability statement in our simulation came from:

where \(\beta_0 = -5.5\) and \(\beta_1 = 0.075\).
